intro: This guide takes your group through “The Mortification of Sin (For Teens)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It retells John Owen’s famous book, first preached to Oxford students and published in 1656, about how a Christian fights the sin that won’t go away. “Mortify” means “put to death”, and Owen’s answer is not grim self-effort but the Holy Spirit and Jesus. It is written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group, especially one ready for honest, serious talk about temptation and growth.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or beforehand at home (8–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens. Because this book is about sin, the most important thing you can do is keep it safe: never ask anyone to name their own sins aloud, keep personal reflection on paper that stays private, and talk in general examples rather than confessions. Some teens carry heavy guilt and some struggle with habits that feel out of control, so keep coming back to Owen’s own centre, the love of Christ and the work of the Spirit. Chapter 4 says plainly that killing sin never means hurting yourself, chapter 9 names habits such as pornography, alcohol, vaping and drugs, and chapter 11 speaks to guilt that will not lift; make sure the group knows they can talk to you or another trusted adult privately, and follow your church’s safeguarding procedures if anyone tells you they are being harmed or harming themselves.

weeks.summary: John Owen, born in 1616, went to Oxford at about twelve, but for years he knew a lot about God without being sure God was his, until an unknown stand-in preacher brought him assurance around 1642. He went on to lead Christ Church and Oxford University, preached to students about sin that wouldn’t go away, and turned those sermons into The Mortification of Sin in 1656, despite later losing his post and all but one of his children. The book’s famous line is “be killing sin or it will be killing you,” but its answer is the Holy Spirit and Jesus, not trying harder. The big idea: this book is for anyone with a sin they keep falling into, and God has real help for them.

memory_verse.text: For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

activity.title: Owen’s Story
steps: Read out the key moments of Owen’s life from the chapter: Oxford at twelve, years of uncertainty, the stand-in preacher, the famous book, the hard losses.
In pairs, talk about why someone who knew so much about God could still lack peace with him.
As a group, put Romans 8:13 into your own words, making sure to keep both “by the Spirit” and “you will live”.
Ask everyone to write privately, on paper they keep, one habit they would like God to help them put to death, and to pray over it during the week.

weeks.summary: Owen builds his book on Romans 8:13 and says that killing sin is daily work for every Christian, even the best, because sin still lives in believers and never takes a day off. He compares it to a gardener who keeps pruning season after season, and warns that someone who stops striking before the enemy is dead has done only half the job. The chapter adds that this is not about being anxious and grim, but about steady training, and that the goal is life. The big idea: be killing sin every day, because the fight leads to life.

memory_verse.text: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.

activity.title: Daily Training
steps: Ask anyone who trains for a sport, a musical instrument or a skill to describe what happens if they stop practising for a month.
Read Owen’s line aloud: “be killing sin or it will be killing you,” and talk about why he compares the Christian life to daily training rather than a one-off effort.
Talk about Owen’s picture of still, deep water, and why sin may be most dangerous when it seems quiet.
Have everyone plan privately a two-minute evening review for this week: thanks for victories, honesty about failures, and a prayer for tomorrow.

weeks.summary: Owen warns that sin always aims at the utmost: an unclean glance would become adultery and a small doubt would become unbelief, if allowed to grow. Sin starts modestly, asking only a little room, then keeps the ground it gains and pushes for more, while we compare ourselves only with last week and think we are not that bad. The chapter is clear that small sins are not as bad as the biggest, but they are seeds, like a snowball that is easiest to stop before it starts rolling. The big idea: take small sins seriously, because sin never wants to stay small.

memory_verse.text: But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.

activity.title: Seed to Snowball
activity.materials: A large sheet of paper and pens
steps: Draw a hill with a small snowball at the top and a huge one at the bottom.
As a group, pick a general example from the chapter, such as a small lie, a bit of jealousy or a flash of irritation.
Fill in the stages down the hill together, showing how it might grow if it were fed every day.
Mark on the drawing the easiest point to stop it, and talk about why.
Ask everyone to think privately of one “small” habit they could stop feeding this week.

weeks.summary: Owen says that trying harder on its own will never kill sin: “A man may easier see without eyes, speak without a tongue, than truly mortify one sin without the Spirit.” Fighting sin in our own strength, by our own methods, to feel good about ourselves, is the heart of false religion, which is why Owen rejected harsh vows and punishing the body. The chapter says very clearly that killing sin never means hurting yourself, and that the fight begins only when a person is joined to Christ by faith and receives his Spirit. The big idea: the power to kill sin is the Holy Spirit’s, so ask for his help instead of only trying harder.

memory_verse.text: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts.

activity.title: Not by Might
steps: List together the ways people try to beat a bad habit by willpower alone, such as resolutions, gritting your teeth or making promises.
Talk about why Owen says these fail on their own, and why harsh self-punishment misses the point entirely.
In pairs, write a short prayer asking the Holy Spirit for strength in the moment of temptation.
Have everyone copy the prayer somewhere they will see it before their usual temptation this week.

weeks.summary: Owen says the vigour, power and comfort of our spiritual life depend on killing sin, which is like pulling weeds that strangle a plant. Unmortified sin weakens and darkens the soul, takes away peace and makes prayer, Bible reading and joy hard, while sin being put to death brings prayer, joy and love back to life. The chapter contrasts sin’s false promises with Jesus’ words about the thief and the abundant life, and recalls Owen’s warning about Christians who grew cold by slowly ceasing to watch. The big idea: killing sin is not losing life but clearing space for it.

memory_verse.text: The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.

activity.title: What Sin Promises
steps: Draw two columns: “What sin promises” and “What sin actually takes”.
As a group, fill in the first column with what temptation often seems to offer, such as fun, freedom or popularity.
Fill in the second column from the chapter, such as peace, joy, prayer and closeness to God.
Read John 10:10 aloud and talk about how Jesus’ promise compares.
Ask everyone to choose privately one practical step against something that drains life from them this week.

weeks.summary: Before saying what killing sin is, Owen lists what it is not: it is not getting rid of sin completely in this life, not merely hiding it, not having a calm personality, not swapping one sin for another, and not a burst of effort after a crisis. Of someone who swaps sins he says, “He hath changed his master, but is a servant still,” and he compares post-crisis calm to an enemy that pulls back to regroup. The chapter adds that a crisis can wake us up, but real change is steadier and deeper. The big idea: real change happens in the heart, not just on the surface.

memory_verse.text: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own.

activity.title: Five Nots
activity.materials: Five slips of paper and pens
steps: Write each of Owen’s five “nots” on a separate slip and lay them out.
Read out a few made-up scenarios, such as someone who stops one bad habit only to start another, and have the group match each to the right “not”.
Talk about which of the five mistakes is easiest for teens to make, keeping to general examples.
Ask everyone to think privately about which “not” might be true of them, and to talk to God about it this week.

weeks.summary: Owen says killing a sin has three parts: weakening its pull so it rises less often and less strongly, constant fighting that includes knowing how the sin works in you and refusing to excuse it, and success, as frequent victories by the Spirit loosen its grip over time. He notes that a sin is often strongest where it fits our temperament or circumstances, so different people face different battles. The chapter stresses that this is a process, more like getting fit than flicking a switch, and that being filled with the Spirit leaves less room for sin. The big idea: walk by the Spirit, and over time sin loses its grip.

memory_verse.text: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.

activity.title: Know Your Enemy
steps: Explain Owen’s three parts: weakening the sin, constant fighting, and success.
As a group, take a general example such as losing your temper, and work out together its usual triggers, its usual excuses and one way to walk by the Spirit at that moment.
Then give everyone a few minutes to do the same privately on paper for a sin they want to fight.
Talk about why the chapter compares this to getting fit rather than flicking a switch.

weeks.summary: Owen warns that someone who fights only the one sin that troubles them, while being careless about prayer, Scripture and how they treat people, will not win, because their real motive is often self-love: they want relief, not holiness. True mortification rests on hatred of sin as sin and “a sense of the love of Christ in the cross,” since Jesus bled for every sin, not only the ones that bother us. Like a sore caused by poor health, one sin is best healed by caring for our whole walk with God. The big idea: ask God to search your whole heart, not just fix one problem.

memory_verse.text: Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!

activity.title: The Whole Garden
steps: Draw a simple garden with several beds labelled prayer, Bible reading, friendships, family, words, and time online.
Talk about Owen’s point that one weedy bed is hard to fix if the rest of the garden is neglected.
Discuss the difference between hating a sin because it makes us feel bad and hating it because it grieves God.
Ask everyone to pray Psalm 139:23–24 quietly and write down privately anything God brings to mind.

weeks.summary: Owen lists warning lights that show a sin has become especially serious: it has gone on a long time, you have made peace with it, it keeps winning, you only resist it for fear of consequences, and God has already warned you and you carried on. When these appear, extraordinary remedies are needed, and one of them is not fighting alone, since Hebrews tells believers to exhort one another daily. The chapter urges anyone whose habit feels out of control, such as pornography, alcohol, vaping or drugs, to talk to a trusted adult, a youth leader or a doctor. The big idea: if the warning lights are flashing, don’t panic and don’t fight alone.

memory_verse.text: But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.

activity.title: Dashboard Check
steps: Draw a car dashboard with five warning lights and label each with one of Owen’s warnings.
Talk about what a sensible driver does when a warning light comes on, and how that compares with sin.
As a group, list the kinds of people a teen could safely talk to about a struggle, and what makes someone trustworthy.
Give everyone a few private minutes to check their own dashboard on paper, and encourage anyone with a flashing light to speak to a trusted adult this week.

weeks.summary: Owen gives two practical pieces of advice: watch against the occasions and opportunities your sin usually uses, and rise against the very first stirrings of temptation without giving it the least ground. He warns against saying “Thus far it shall go, and no farther,” because sin given one step takes another, like water that runs its course once it breaks out of a channel. The chapter applies this to ordinary life, such as not keeping your phone in your room at night if that is where you fall. The big idea: change the situation and turn away in the first few seconds.

memory_verse.text: Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

activity.title: Danger Zones
steps: As a group, list common times and places where teens face temptation, such as late at night, being bored or lonely, certain apps or certain group chats.
For each, brainstorm one practical change that would make it easier to say no.
Talk about Owen’s warning against letting temptation in “just a crack”.
Ask everyone to write privately their own top two danger situations and one change for each.

weeks.summary: Owen urges believers to take sin seriously by talking honestly to themselves, asking how they can face the Lord Jesus and whether they will grieve the Spirit who sealed them, so that Christ’s love makes sin look as ugly as it is. He also warns against speaking peace to ourselves before God speaks it, grabbing a quick “it doesn’t matter” instead of truly turning; our part is to confess, turn and trust, and giving peace is God’s. The chapter is clear that God loves to speak peace and does forgive, and that anyone who can never feel forgiven should talk to a pastor or trusted adult. The big idea: real peace comes from God, and it goes together with real change.

memory_verse.text: Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly.

activity.title: Real Peace, Fake Peace
steps: Draw a road with a ditch on each side, labelled “It doesn’t matter” and “I’ll never be forgiven”.
As a group, write in the middle of the road the steps Owen describes: confess honestly, turn from it, trust Christ, receive his peace.
Read 1 John 1:9 together and talk about how it keeps us out of both ditches.
Remind everyone that if guilt ever feels stuck, a pastor or trusted adult can help.

weeks.summary: Owen’s most important direction is to set faith to work on Christ, whose blood is the great remedy for sin-sick souls, with the promise that we will live to see our sin dead at our feet. Even when we are weary of fighting, there is enough in Christ, as the prodigal remembered there was bread enough in his father’s house, and looking at Jesus on the cross makes sin look ugly and freedom desirable. Two days before his death in 1683, Owen wrote that he was going to him “who hath loved me with an everlasting love.” The big idea: the fight against sin ends not with our willpower but with Christ’s love, so keep looking at Jesus.

memory_verse.text: Looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.

activity.title: Looking at Jesus
steps: Read Luke 23:33–46 aloud slowly while everyone listens.
Give everyone two quiet minutes to write down one thing they noticed about Jesus in the passage.
Read Owen’s last letter aloud and talk about why he corrected himself from “whom my soul hath loved” to “who hath loved me”.
Look back over the twelve weeks and ask each person to name, if they wish, one thing they have learned about fighting sin.
